title: Nobody Warned You That Ulaanbaatar Skipped the Card Machine Era
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_markdown:
Ask ten travelers what to expect from money in Mongolia and you will hear ten versions of the same story: bring a brick of cash, guard it with your life, and hope the one ATM in town is working. Some of that story is still true. A surprising amount of it is not. Mongolia in 2026 is really two payment worlds living side by side, and if you only prepare for one of them, you will either carry far too much cash in the capital or far too little in the countryside.


So let's go through the beliefs one at a time, the way you would fact-check a friend who last visited in 2012.


### Belief one: Mongolia is a cash-only country


Walk down Peace Avenue in Ulaanbaatar and count how many times you see someone tap their phone at a till. Coffee shops, pharmacies, supermarkets, the food courts near Sukhbaatar Square, even small kiosks selling khuushuur: QR codes are everywhere. Locals pay through bank apps and wallets like QPay, SocialPay, and Monpay, and for many younger residents of the capital, a day without touching a banknote is completely normal.


The QR sticker taped next to the register is not decoration. It is often the merchant's preferred way to get paid, because it settles instantly and nobody has to count change. If your mental image of Mongolia's payment scene is a drawer full of crumpled tugrik notes, update it. Ulaanbaatar largely jumped past the card terminal era and went straight to phones.


### Belief two: fine, then my Visa or Mastercard will handle everything


This is the opposite mistake, and it is just as expensive. Card terminals exist in Ulaanbaatar, mostly in hotels, larger restaurants, and chain supermarkets, but they are far from universal, and foreign cards get declined often enough that you should never rely on one as your only plan. The smaller and more local the place, the more likely your only two options are a QR code or cash.


Mongolia is also one of the countries where internationally-friendly payment options are genuinely thin on the ground. There is no easy visitor onramp into the local wallets, and the big regional super-apps that work elsewhere in Asia do not help you here. Travelers who breeze through Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur on cards and wallets are frequently surprised by how few of their usual tools function in Ulaanbaatar.


### Belief three: those QR codes are for locals only


Here is where the story usually ends for visitors. QPay and its cousins are built around Mongolian bank accounts and Mongolian phone numbers, so travelers tend to look at the QR sticker, sigh, and go find an ATM. That was the correct move for years. It no longer has to be.


Moreta Pay lets you scan the same standard QR codes locals use, straight from your own phone, with no Mongolian bank account and no local SIM registration dance. You fund the wallet from home (a US bank via Plaid or ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card) in your own currency. At the register you scan the merchant's code, see the amount in tugrik, the exchange rate, and the merchant's name on your screen, then confirm. The merchant is paid instantly in tugrik, you keep a clean digital record, and you earn 1% cash back on the purchase. For a country with so few visitor-friendly options, being able to simply join the local QR system changes the whole trip.


### Belief four: the countryside works the same as the city


It absolutely does not, and this is the myth that gets travelers into real trouble. The moment you leave Ulaanbaatar for Terelj, Kharkhorin, the Gobi, or a ger camp anywhere on the steppe, assume cash. Herder families selling airag by the road, small guanz canteens in provincial towns, drivers, guides, entrance fees at remote sites: tugrik notes, please. Mobile coverage can vanish for hours at a time, and no payment app on earth works without a signal.


The smart pattern is a hybrid one. Withdraw or exchange the cash you will actually need for your countryside days before you leave the capital, and handle everything in Ulaanbaatar itself by QR. That keeps your cash pile small, which matters because pulling tugrik from machines as a foreigner is not free, something we broke down in detail in[our guide to what tugrik withdrawals really cost visitors](https://moretapay.com/blog/mongolia-atm-fees-exchange-rates-tugrik-faq-2026-2026-08-26) . Every purchase you move from cash to QR in the city is one fewer trip to the ATM.


### Belief five: I can sort all of this out after I land


Partially true, and partially a trap. You can exchange money and find ATMs after landing, sure. But Chinggis Khaan International Airport is not the place to build your whole payment strategy, and if you arrive on a Friday evening before a long weekend or during Naadam in July, banks will be closed and queues will be long. Naadam is also exactly when you want frictionless payments, because you will be buying tickets, snacks, and souvenirs in crowds where fumbling with an unfamiliar currency is no fun at all.


Set up before you fly: install Moreta Pay, connect your home bank or card, and top up the wallet while you are still on good WiFi. Then your first hours in Ulaanbaatar are spent eating buuz, not standing in a currency exchange line doing mental math.


### Belief six: QR is just for shops


One more underrated point. QR-based payment is not limited to the physical till. If you are booking parts of your trip through platforms like Trip.com or Agoda, QR checkout options let you pay from the same wallet, at the same transparent rate, instead of exposing your home card to another round of foreign transaction fees. Digital nomads settling into Ulaanbaatar for a season will also appreciate being able to handle QR-based bills without a local account. Mongolia's payment culture has more in common with its neighbors than most visitors expect; if your route includes China, the QR-first logic there is even more extreme, as we covered in[why your Visa card won't save you in Shanghai](https://moretapay.com/blog/china-money-myths-wechat-pay-qr-avoid-atm-fees-2026-2026-08-26) .


### The honest summary for your packing list


Bring some cash, but only for the steppe. In Ulaanbaatar, the phone in your pocket can do what the locals' phones do: scan the sticker, check the tugrik amount and the rate on screen, tap confirm, walk out. No local bank account, no hidden foreign transaction fees, no ATM anxiety in a country famous for it.
